title.en: The Birth of Diarmuid and the Druid's Boar
title.zh: 迪爾穆德之誕生與德魯伊的野豬

region.en: Brugh na Boinne (Newgrange), Co. Meath, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭米斯郡博因墓丘

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VI, ch. I, eBook #14465

summary.en: Diarmuid, son of Donn and near of kin to Finn, is reared by Angus Og at Brugh na Boinne together with the Steward's son. In a quarrel of hounds Donn squeezes the Steward's child to death between his knees; when divination and destroying-bonds force out the truth, the Steward strokes his own dead son into a bristle-less, earless, tailless wild boar and binds him to bring Diarmuid to his death — the Boar of Slieve Guillion that will kill him at the last.
summary.zh: 迪爾穆德——東恩之子、芬恩近親——由安古斯·奧格於博因墓丘撫養，與總管之子同育。群犬爭食之亂中，東恩以雙膝擠斃總管之子；占卜與毀滅之誓逼出真相後，總管以德魯伊杖將亡兒化為無鬃、無耳、無尾的野豬，並命其必致迪爾穆德於死——即日後殺他的「古利昂山野豬」。

sensitivity.note: The doom-boar is the frame of the Diarmuid cycle (destiny imposed at birth by a wronged party); Finn's divination by chessboard and basin of pale gold recurs across the corpus. Newgrange pin for Angus's household.

passages.text: Diarmuid was son of Donn, son of Duibhne of the Fianna, and his mother was Crochnuit, that was near in blood to Finn. At the time he was born, Donn was banished from the Fianna because of some quarrel, and Angus Og took the child to rear him up at Brugh na Boinne. After a while Crochnuit bore another son to Roc Diocain, that was Head Steward to Angus, and Angus took that child into Brugh na Boinne, and he and Diarmuid were reared up together. One day Finn was on the great Hill at Almhuin, and Bran Beag came in and asked did he remember there were bonds on him not to stop in Almhuin for ten nights together, and Donn said: "I will bring you to the house of Angus, son of the Dagda, where my young son is being reared."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Steward's son was made as much of as Angus made of Diarmuid, and there was great vexation on Donn when he saw that. It chanced a great fight rose between two of Finn's hounds about some broken meat, and in running away the Steward's child ran between the knees of Donn, and Donn gave the child a strong squeeze between his two knees that killed him on the moment, and threw him under the feet of the hounds. When the Steward came and found his son dead he cried out to Finn: "What satisfaction will I get from you for that?" "Try can you find the mark of a tooth or of a nail of one of the hounds on him, and if you can, I will give you satisfaction for him." There was no scratch or mark of a tooth on him at all; and the Steward put Finn under the destroying bonds of the Druid cave of Cruachan to give him knowledge of who it was killed his son, and Finn searched in a basin of pale gold and it was shown him truly that it was Donn had killed the Steward's son between his two knees.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the Steward came again, having a Druid rod with him, and he struck his own son with the rod, and he made of him a wild boar, without bristle or ear or tail, and he said: "I put you under bonds to bring Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne, to his death; and your own life will be no longer than his life." With that the wild boar rose up and ran out of the open door, and he was called afterwards the Boar of Slieve Guillion, and it was by him Diarmuid came to his death at the last.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. I; not verbatim.

title.en: The Wether That Was the World and Youth's Love-Spot
title.zh: 即為世界的公羊與青春之愛斑

region.en: Slieve Bladhma woods, Co. Tipperary, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭蒂珀雷里郡布洛馬山林地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VI, ch. II, eBook #14465

summary.en: Stormed in at midnight, Diarmuid, Conan, Goll and Osgar wrestle in turn with a wether that throws each of them — until an old man's cat ties it up. "The strength of the world is in the wether, but death will come to the world itself," the host explains, showing the cat. In the night Youth, the beautiful girl of the house, refuses Conan, Osgar and Diarmuid alike — she belonged to them once and never again — but she sets her hand on Diarmuid's forehead and leaves the love-spot no woman can refuse her love to.
summary.zh: 午夜投宿，迪爾穆德、科南、戈爾、奧斯加輪流與一頭公羊角力而皆被摔翻——直到老者的貓將其縛住。「世界之力在公羊，然而死亡終將臨於世界本身。」主人展示貓道破天機。夜裡，屋中名為「青春」的美少女一一回絕科南、奧斯加、迪爾穆德——她曾屬於他們，此生不再——卻將手按於迪爾穆德額上，留下無女子能拒其愛的愛斑。

sensitivity.note: The wether-is-the-world, cat-is-death allegory is a memento-mori parable of the cycle (compare Cuanna's house); the love-spot (ball seirce) is Diarmuid's fixed device and the engine of the Grania pursuit. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: Diarmuid and Conan and Goll and Osgar went one day hunting, and they went so far they could not get home in the evening, and when it was about midnight they saw a light, and found a little house, and went in. They saw an old man there that bade them welcome and called them all by their names, and no one in the house but the old man and a young girl and a cat. When the food was ready and put on the table, there came a great wether that was fastened up in the back of the house, and he rose up on the table where they were eating.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: "Rise up, Conan, and fasten that wether in the place it was before." Conan took hold of it, but the wether gave itself a shake that threw Conan under one of its feet; and Diarmuid rose up and was thrown down the same way; and Osgar got up, but the wether put him down under one of his feet, so that it had now the three men under him. Then Goll rose up and took hold of it and threw it down; but it rose up again in spite of him, and put Goll under his fourth foot.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: "It is a great shame the like of that to be done to the Fianna of Ireland. And rise up now, cat, and tie the wether in the place where he was." The cat rose up then and took hold of the wether, and brought it over and tied it in its place. "When you are done I will show you that now you are the bravest men of the world. Goll, you are the bravest of all the men of the world, for you have wrestled with the world and you threw it down. The strength of the world is in the wether, but death will come to the world itself; and that is death," he said, showing them the cat. The four of them went into the one room to sleep, and the young girl came to sleep in the same room with them, and it was Youth the young girl was.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: "Go back to your bed, Conan; I belonged to you once, and I will never belong to you again." "Go back again, Osgar; I belonged to you once, and I will never belong to you again." Then Diarmuid rose up to go to her: "O Diarmuid, that cannot be; I belonged to you once, and I can never belong to you again; but come over here to me, and I will put a love-spot on you, that no woman will ever see without giving you her love." So Diarmuid went over to her, and she put her hand on his forehead, and she left the love-spot there, and no woman that ever saw him after that was able to refuse him her love.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. II; not verbatim.

title.en: The Wild Woman and the House on the Hillside
title.zh: 野性女子與山坡上的華屋

region.en: Valley near the Brosna, Co. Offaly, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭奧法利郡布羅斯納河谷（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VI, ch. III, eBook #14465

summary.en: On a snowy midnight a wild ugly woman with hair to her heels begs shelter from Finn and Oisin in turn and is refused; Diarmuid lets her in, and by the fire she is a beautiful young woman asleep. In the morning a great house stands ready on the hillside; she warns Diarmuid never to remind her of how she came to him. He visits the Fianna three days running, and each time one of them wins a pup of his greyhound from her — until on the third recall of her ugliness the house and the woman vanish and he wakes on bare ground.
summary.zh: 雪夜裡，一頭髮及踵的醜野女先後向芬恩、歐辛求宿而被拒；迪爾穆德容她入內，火畔她已是睡著的美少女。晨起，山坡上華屋已成；她囑迪爾穆德永不可提她初來時的模樣。他三度回訪菲亞納同伴，每次皆有人從她處贏得愛犬幼崽——第三次他重提其醜態，華屋與女子霎時消失，他醒於荒地。

sensitivity.note: The loathly-lady (ugly woman who becomes beautiful through generosity) is the international ATU motif D732 here in its Irish form; the broken taboo of recalling her ugliness is the release-clause. Compare Finn and the loathly lady of the same family of tales.

passages.text: One snowy night of winter the Fianna were come into the house after their hunting, and about midnight they heard a knocking at the door, and there came in a woman very wild and ugly, and her hair hanging to her heels. She asked Finn to let her in under the border of his covering, and when he saw her so strange and so wild-looking he would not let her in; and Oisin refused her the same way. Then she went over where Diarmuid was: "You are strange-looking and wild and ugly, and your hair is down to your heels. But come in for all that," he said.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: "O Diarmuid, I have been travelling over sea and ocean through the length of seven years, and in all that time I never got shelter any night till this night." He brought her over to the fire, and all the Fianna went away from it seeing her so ugly and so dreadful to look at; and she asked to come under the warmth of the covering with him, and he turned a fold of it between them. But it was not long till he looked at her, and what he saw was a beautiful young woman beside him, and she asleep.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: "Where would you like to see the best house built that ever was built?" she said; and in the morning two men of the Fianna came in and said they were after seeing a great house up on the hill where there was not a house before. "I will go to it, if you will come along with me." "I will do that, if you will make me a promise not to say to me three times what way I was when I came to you." They went up to the house, and everything they could wish for they had it. She bade him go to his comrades, and Diarmuid took leave of her and went back to the Fianna, and there was a great welcome before him; but for all that they were someway envious, Diarmuid to have got that grand house and her love from the woman they themselves had turned away.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: Finn came towards her and asked one of the pups of Diarmuid's greyhound bitch, and she gave it; and Oisin came, and Caoilte, and each got a pup the same way. But every time Diarmuid came home and found a pup gone, he said it was because she remembered the way she was when she came to him; and the third time the house was gone and the woman was gone on the moment, and it was on the bare ground he awoke on the morrow. There was great sorrow on him then, and he said he would search in every place till he would find her again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Cup of the Plain of Wonder and the Healing That Ended Love
title.zh: 奇觀平原之杯與終結愛情的治癒

region.zh: 浪下之國，西海（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VI, ch. III, eBook #14465

summary.en: Searching for the vanished woman, Diarmuid rides a ship below the sea to Land-under-Wave, where the King's daughter is sick for love of him — she lost a drop of heart's blood at every thought of him on her seven-year enchanted journey. Her cure demands three draughts from the cup of the King of the Plain of Wonder, which no man ever got; Diarmuid destroys two armies, learns he was prophesied seven years before his birth, and takes the cup — but the red man, the messenger from beyond the world, warns that the healing will take his love with it, and so it does.
summary.zh: 尋找消失的女子，迪爾穆德乘船入海底之國「浪下之國」。國王之女正因思念他而病——七年魔困之旅中，每念他一次便失一滴心血。痊癒需奇觀平原之王之杯中的三口酒，而此杯無人可得；迪爾穆德殲滅兩軍，方知其毀滅早於出生七年已被預言。然而「界外信使」紅人警示：治癒之時，愛亦將隨之而去——果然如此。

sensitivity.note: The cup-of-healing quest under the sea is the Fenian grail-quest analogue; the love-destroying cure inverts the usual magical-healing plot and is a rare narrative device (love lost through the very act of saving the beloved). The messenger-from-beyond-the-world is a deus ex machina of the vision genre.

passages.text: Diarmuid followed the path she took down to the strand, and then he saw a ship, and leaned on the handle of his spear and made a light leap on to it; and the boat went out over the sea, and then down below it, and Diarmuid found himself on a plain. He met with three drops of blood on the way and put them in a napkin — the greyhound had lost them. He saw a woman gathering rushes: "The daughter of King Under-Wave is come home, and she was for seven years under enchantment, and there is sickness on her now, and all the physicians are gathered together and none of them can do her any good, and a bed of rushes is what she finds the wholesomest." The woman put the rushes about him and carried him to her on her back, and they took one another's hands, and were very joyful at that meeting. "Three parts of my sickness is gone from me now; but I am not well yet, and I never will be, for every time I thought of you, Diarmuid, on my journey, I lost a drop of the blood of my heart." "It is three draughts from the cup of the King of Magh an Ionganaidh, the Plain of Wonder, and no man ever got it or ever will get it."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: Diarmuid came to the little river before the Plain of Wonder, and there was a low-sized reddish man standing in the middle of it: "Come here and put your foot in the palm of my hand and I will bring you through." At the king's dun Diarmuid called out that the cup should be sent out to him, or champions to fight with him; twice eight hundred fighting men were sent, and in three hours there was not one of them left to stand against him; twice nine hundred better fighters again, and within four hours there was not one of them left. Then the King of the Plain of Wonder came out: "Where did the man come from that has brought destruction on the whole of my kingdom? For seven years before you were born it was put in the prophecy that you would come to destroy them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: And it is easy for me to give you the cup, whether or not there is healing in it." And the red man brought him back over the river: "I am the messenger from beyond the world, and I came to your help because your own heart is hot to come to the help of another. When you come where the woman is, put the water of the well in the cup, and one of the drops of blood in it, and she will drink it, and the same with the second drop and the third, and her sickness will be gone from her from that time. But there is another thing will be gone along with it, and that is the love you have for her." "That will not go from me," said Diarmuid. "It will go from you."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: So Diarmuid did as he bade him, and he brought the water and the cup and the drops of blood to the woman, and she drank them, and at the third draught she was healed. And no sooner was she healed than the love he had for her was gone, and he turned away from her. "O Diarmuid, your love is gone from me." "O, it is gone indeed," said he. Then there was music made in the whole place, and the lamenting was stopped, because of the healing of the king's daughter. And as to Diarmuid, he would take no reward and he would not stop there, but he asked for a ship to bring him home to Ireland, to Finn and the Fianna, and when he came where they were, there was a joyful welcome before him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. III; not verbatim.

title.en: The Gilla Decair and the Horse That Broke the Fianna
title.zh: 劣僕與拖垮菲亞納的怪馬

region.zh: 愛爾蘭利默里克郡艾妮·克利亞

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VI, ch. IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: A huge gloomy Fomorian calls himself the Gilla Decair, the Hard Servant, comes to Finn for wages, and turns his starveling horse loose among the Fianna's horses to tear and kill. Conan, forced into horse-boy's service, mounts it with twelve men behind him and it will not stir; the Fomor taunts them and walks away slow — then tucks up his cloak and is gone like a swallow, leaving thirteen of the Fianna clinging to the horse that streams after him, the opening of the pursuit that ends in Tir fo Thuinn.
summary.zh: 一名陰鬱巨人自稱「劣僕」，前來芬恩處求佣，卻將其瘦骨嶙峋的怪馬放至菲亞納馬群中撕咬殘殺。科南被迫充當馬伕，攜十二人騎上怪馬，馬卻紋絲不動。弗莫爾譏嘲後慢步離開——隨即撩起斗篷，疾如飛燕而去，菲亞納十三人被怪馬拖拽緊追其後——一場終至「浪下之國」的大追逐就此開啟。

sensitivity.note: The Gilla Decair cycle (Acallam-material) is the source of the Land-under-Wave pursuit; Manannan is elsewhere identified with this trickster-figure in the corpus (Gregory's own remark). The wages-servant ruse is a fixed folktale opening (Aarne-Thompson 'work-avoidance servant'). Pin at Aine Cliach where the hunt stood.

passages.text: The Fianna went hunting one time in the two proud provinces of Munster, through the borders of Magh Breogain, over the level banks of the blue Siuir and over the green plain of Feman. Finn asked which of the men that were with him would go and keep watch on the side of the hill where they were, and Finnbane, son of Bresel, went; and he saw coming from the east a very big man, ugly and gloomy and deformed, a dark-coloured shield on his back, a wide sword on his crooked left thigh, his limbs as black as a quenched coal, leading a sulky bony horse by a rough iron halter, and striking blows on it with an iron cudgel to try and knock some going out of him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: He saluted Finn, making signs of humility: "I am a man of the Fomor, travelling in search of wages to the kings of the earth, and I heard that Finn never refused wages to any man. There is nothing in the world is worse to me than a boy to be with me, for it is a hundred men's share of food that serves me for one day. The name I have is the Gilla Decair, the Hard Servant." And he turned his horse loose among the horses of the Fianna, and it began to tear and to kick and to bite at them, killing and maiming.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: "I will never bring him out of that; for I have no serving-boy to do it for me, and it is not work for me to be leading my horse by the hand." Conan rose up then and took the halter and put it on the horse: "You would never have done a horse-boy's service, Conan, to any one of the Fianna," said Finn; "if you will do what I advise, you will get up on the horse now and search out with him all the hills and hollows of Ireland, till his heart is broken in his body." Conan made a leap on to the horse and thirteen men of the Fianna went up behind him, but with all that the horse would not stir, and the big man went from them slow and weak, dragging himself along till he had put a little hill between himself and the Fianna; and as soon as he was on the other side of it, he tucked up his cloak to his waist, and away with him as if with the quickness of a swallow or a deer.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.
